lead.headline: Hawaiʻi conditionally clears Navy ʻAiea Hālawa drinking-water shaft for reactivation
lead.summary: The Hawaiʻi Department of Health says the Navy may reactivate the ʻAiea Hālawa Shaft only after required treatment, testing and advance customer notification conditions are met.
lead.why_it_matters: The decision affects the resilience of the Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam water system, which serves about 93,000 users, while keeping monitoring and enforcement requirements in place.
body: The Hawaiʻi Department of Health has conditionally approved the Navy’s request to reactivate the ʻAiea Hālawa Shaft as a drinking-water source for the Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam public water system. The department says the additional source is intended to improve system resilience by supplementing the Waiawa Shaft, which regulators had identified as a single-source vulnerability for a system serving about 93,000 users.

The approval is conditional, not an immediate or unrestricted return to service. DOH required granular activated carbon treatment, ion-exchange treatment and disinfection systems, along with sampling points for continued testing. The department said testing covered more than 50 contaminants, including PFAS and total petroleum hydrocarbons, and did not find them above applicable regulatory standards.

PFAS had been detected at the shaft in June 2024, so the Navy was also required to demonstrate that the installed treatment could remove those compounds. The Navy must operate the system under state and federal drinking-water laws and report within 24 hours any condition that could contaminate the source.

DOH emphasized that the Navy’s ʻAiea Hālawa Shaft is not the Navy’s Red Hill Shaft or the Honolulu Board of Water Supply’s Hālawa Shaft. The agency said the source is about two miles from the Red Hill facility and that a geologic barrier, the expected low pumping rate and continued pumping at the Red Hill Shaft make an effect on underground contamination unlikely under the approved conditions.

Before reactivation, the Navy must notify its customers and DOH at least 10 days in advance. DOH says it will continue monitoring groundwater data and may suspend or revoke the approval if conditions are not met or if a future public-health threat is identified. Readers served by the system should rely on official Navy and DOH notices for the actual start date and any customer instructions.

stories.headline: PAGASA: Localized thunderstorms possible across the Philippines on September 13
stories.summary: PAGASA forecasts partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms across most of the country, with easterlies affecting the far north.
stories.why_it_matters: Families and travelers should expect mostly localized weather but remain alert because severe thunderstorms can still trigger flash floods or landslides.
body: The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration says localized thunderstorms may bring isolated rainshowers across much of the Philippines on Sunday, September 13. The national forecast was issued at 4:00 a.m. Philippine time and describes partly cloudy to cloudy conditions for Metro Manila and most other areas.

PAGASA says easterlies are affecting Batanes and the Babuyan Islands, where isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms are also possible. For Metro Manila and the rest of the country, localized thunderstorms are the main weather driver rather than a single nationwide rain system.

Even when rain is isolated, PAGASA cautions that severe thunderstorms can produce flash floods or landslides. Conditions can vary sharply over short distances, so residents should check regional warnings and local government advisories before travel, outdoor events or trips through flood- and landslide-prone areas.

The agency forecasts light to moderate winds. Coastal waters are expected to be slight to moderate, at about 1.2 to 2.1 meters in Extreme Northern Luzon and roughly 0.6 to 1.5 meters elsewhere. Local marine bulletins should still be checked because thunderstorm conditions can change quickly.

For Hawaiʻi families coordinating with relatives or travelers in the Philippines, the practical takeaway is to plan for brief, localized downpours rather than assume uniform rain nationwide. Monitor PAGASA’s current forecast and regional advisories, and avoid flooded roads or unstable slopes if a strong thunderstorm develops.
